1.pericope_label: Moreover the spirit lifted me up, and brought me unto the east gate of the Lord’s house, which looketh eastward: and behold at the door of the gate five and twenty men; among whom I saw Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. Then said he unto me, Son of man, these are the men that devise mischief, and give wicked counsel in this city:

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter into judgment on the rulers, the promise to the exiles, and the withdrawal of the presence, and render the agent that lifts the prophet a wind. Ellicott traces the movement from the court of the priests to the main outer entrance where the cherubim had gone, keeps open the question whether these twenty-five are the twenty-five already seen, offers two readings of the number, and presses the etymologies of the two names as chosen to expose the people's false hopes.

Gill has the prophet lifted from the inner court by the same Spirit that once took him by a lock of his head. Calvin makes the leaders the cause of the ruin, since if the blind lead the blind both fall into the ditch, declines any arithmetic of the number as a definite put for an indefinite, explains that ordinary men treat their rulers as a shield and throw off blame under pretence of ignorance, and draws from the prophet's boldness the rule that rank confers no immunity from censure.

Clarke divides the chapter as Keil and Delitzsch do, has no doubt the twenty-five are the same men seen worshipping the sun, and weighs whether the Jaazaniah here is the Jaazaniah of the earlier chapter. Wesley keeps the two men distinct and notes that Pelatiah is named for the sake of the sudden death that made him a warning.

Henry insists these are princes sitting in the gate to try causes, not the priests seen earlier, and charged with maladministration rather than corrupt worship; he reports the tradition of twenty-four city wards with their president, and reads the counsel as advice to silence the prophets, rebel against Babylon and hold out to the last extremity.

debates.question: Are these twenty-five men the twenty-five seen earlier worshipping the sun?

positions.position: The same persons, no doubt.
Not the same: those were priests or Levites between the porch and the altar, these are princes sitting in the gate to try causes and charged with maladministration.
Generally supposed different, one set priestly and one secular, but the question cannot be closed, since the same idolatrous priests may have gained an ascendancy over the people.

debates.question: What does the number twenty-five signify?

positions.position: Either the king with two princes from each of the twelve tribes, or nothing beyond a considerable array of the most prominent men.
The governors of twenty-four city wards with their president.
A definite number put for an indefinite; what matters is only that the rulers were despisers of God.

debates.question: Is this Jaazaniah the Jaazaniah named in the earlier vision?

positions.position: Probably two men of the name, both chiefs, though they might be one if Shaphan was also called Azur.
Not the same man, the one being son of Shaphan and this one son of Azur.

outliers.claim: Presses the meanings of the names -- the Lord hears, the helper, God rescues, the Lord builds -- as chosen to bring out the false hopes with which the people beguiled themselves, which is what made the sudden death so impressive.

Explains why the charge had to be laid on the rulers by name: ordinary men treat their commanders as a shield and think themselves guiltless so long as they obeyed, throwing off all blame under pretence of ignorance.

themes: Moreover the spirit lifted me up, and brought me unto the east gate of the Lord’s house, which looketh eastward: and behold at the door of the gate five and twenty men; among whom I saw Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.
Then said he unto me, Son of man, these are the men that devise mischief, and give wicked counsel in this city:

3.pericope_label: Which say, It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh. Therefore prophesy against them, prophesy, O son of man. And the Spirit of the Lord fell upon me, and said unto me, Speak; Thus saith the Lord; Thus have ye said, O house of Israel: for I know the things that come into your mind, every one of them. Ye have multiplied your slain in this city, and ye have filled the streets thereof with the slain. Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that either the text or the margin renders the original accurately: it is literally not near to build houses, and it is a retort against the letter telling the exiles to build because the captivity would be long. He reads the caldron as the princes' own figure of walls protecting the flesh within, and answers that the city would secure only the dead while the living were handed to the stranger; violence, he adds, is the natural fruit of defection.

Gill records two further renderings the Hebrew will bear and rejects both as prudent rather than wicked counsel, and counts among the slain both the prophets they killed and everyone who died in the siege through their advice to hold out. Calvin develops the scoff at length, has the prophet answer jest with jest -- the pot is already full and there is no room left -- widens the charge of bloodshed to every form of injustice, and draws from the Spirit falling afresh the rule that a gift must be renewed at every exercise.

Clarke takes the plain sense that the invasion is not near, allows the caldron saying to be either a resolve to share the city's fate or open ridicule of an earlier vision, and says the men shall not be allowed to stay and share it. Wesley calls the saying an impious scoff with some fear in it, holds the princes answerable for everyone the Chaldeans killed, and notes that being brought forth is wrath and not mercy.

debates.question: What do the princes mean by saying it is not near?

positions.position: That the threatened invasion is not near.
The same, though the Hebrew will also bear that it is not proper to build near the city or inside it; both readings are rejected as prudent rather than wicked counsel.
Literally not near to build houses: a retort denying the letter that told the exiles to build because the captivity would be long.

debates.question: What is the force of the caldron saying?

positions.position: The city's walls will keep the flesh inside safe from the fire of any attack.
Either a resolve to stay and share the city's fate, or ridicule of an earlier vision of a seething pot.
A pretended inconsistency: if they are the flesh in the pot they are meant to stay, so the threat of exile contradicts the figure; and they expected only a light scorching.

debates.question: Who are the slain that fill the city?

positions.position: The prophets they killed and the innocent they condemned, together with all who died in the siege through their advice to hold out.
Not necessarily men openly put to death: the phrase covers every form of injustice, since God reckons as homicides those who oppress the wretched and overturn their fortunes.

outliers.claim: Draws a rule from the Spirit falling afresh on a man already endued with prophecy: the grace had to be renewed at every exercise of it, since one illumination is not enough unless God works daily, and the point of insisting on it is that the words are dictated and not the prophet's own.
Reconstructs the quarrel behind the retort, that a false prophet among the exiles wrote to Jerusalem demanding the punishment of the man who had told them to settle down for a long captivity.

themes: Which say, It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh.
Therefore prophesy against them, prophesy, O son of man.
And the Spirit of the Lord fell upon me, and said unto me, Speak; Thus saith the Lord; Thus have ye said, O house of Israel: for I know the things that come into your mind, every one of them.
Ye have multiplied your slain in this city, and ye have filled the streets thereof with the slain.
Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it.

8.pericope_label: Ye have feared the sword; and I will bring a sword upon you, saith the Lord God. And I will bring you out of the midst thereof, and deliver you into the hands of strangers, and will execute judgments among you. Ye shall fall by the sword; I will judge you in the border of Israel; and ye shall know that I am the Lord. This city shall not be your caldron, neither shall ye be the flesh in the midst thereof; but I will judge you in the border of Israel: And ye shall know that I am the Lord: for ye have not walked in my statutes, neither executed my judgments, but have done after the manners of the heathen that are round about you. And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then fell I down upon my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said, Ah Lord God! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the sentence as cumulative -- first the sword, then expulsion and delivery to strangers, then arraignment in the border, which would be most terrible of all to a Jew -- points to the fulfilment at Riblah on the northern confines, and observes that the recognition of the Lord came not through repentance but through undergoing the judgments; he identifies Pelatiah as one of the princes already named and notes that the prophet turns at once to intercession.

Gill keeps the caldron figure running: they are brought out of the city they had called their pot, they fall by the sword outside the walls rather than within, and the city is a caldron for the dead and not the living. Calvin answers the objection the figure invites, that being drawn out does not falsify the earlier prophecy since God never restricted his wrath to one kind of punishment; he holds that Pelatiah died at the time of the vision, makes his fall a prelude to the general destruction, and finds the outcry sharpened by the man's name, whose root means to escape.

Clarke fixes the border on Riblah, in Syria but on the frontier, where the king's sons were slain and his eyes put out, refers the strangers chiefly to the royal family, and thinks Pelatiah was most probably struck dead the very hour the prophet spoke. Wesley explains the same geography, says the judgment will pursue them wherever they fly, and reads the death as done in vision only, as an assurance of what would follow in fact.

debates.question: Did Pelatiah actually die at that moment?

positions.position: Most probably struck dead the very hour the prophet spoke, like the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira.
He died at the time of the vision, though possibly at his own house rather than the temple threshold, since a vision is not limited to places.
Done now in vision only, as an assurance that it would be done in fact when the prophecy was published.

debates.question: Does the deportation falsify the earlier caldron prophecy?

positions.position: No: the Chaldeans would consume them wherever they were, and God never restricted his wrath to one kind of punishment, the prophets using various figures.
No: the caldron holds, but for the dead, not for the living, who fall outside the walls.

debates.question: Why does the outcry take the form it does?

positions.position: The prophet is greatly affected by the sudden death of a named prince and intercedes that God not make a full end of the remnant.
He speaks not from prophetic knowledge but according to the common opinion, which held that the city's stability rested on this man's counsel.

outliers.claim: Finds a play on the name behind the outcry: the root means to escape and yields the word for survivors, so the very man whose name held out escape is the one taken.

Notes that being arraigned in the border, at the extremity of the land or outside it, was the part of the sentence most terrible to a Jew, and locates it historically at Riblah on the northern confines.

themes: Ye have feared the sword; and I will bring a sword upon you, saith the Lord God.
And I will bring you out of the midst thereof, and deliver you into the hands of strangers, and will execute judgments among you.
Ye shall fall by the sword; I will judge you in the border of Israel; and ye shall know that I am the Lord.
This city shall not be your caldron, neither shall ye be the flesh in the midst thereof; but I will judge you in the border of Israel:
And ye shall know that I am the Lord: for ye have not walked in my statutes, neither executed my judgments, but have done after the manners of the heathen that are round about you.

And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then fell I down upon my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said, Ah Lord God! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?

14.pericope_label: Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, thy brethren, even thy brethren, the men of thy kindred, and all the house of Israel wholly, are they unto whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, Get you far from the Lord: unto us is this land given in possession. Therefore say, Thus saith the Lord God; Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come.

schools.summary: Ellicott insists this is the answer to the intercession and not a new prophecy, and marks how completely it turns from the city to the exiles; he explains the kinsman language by the office of the next of kin, notes that the exiles are then called the whole house of Israel so that the others are the cast out, and denies that little is an adjective at all, reading a sanctuary for a little while, for the term of the captivity.

Gill renders the phrase men of thy redemption, records that the Greek translators mistook it and reports a rabbinic view referring the three phrases to three deportations. Calvin reads a rebuke into the answer -- the Church does not perish when the conspicuous are removed -- refuses to take the Jerusalemites' words as a command, and turns the passage into a rule against measuring the Church by common opinion or visible splendour, since it is often preserved in hiding places among people of no estimation.

Clarke quotes the city's boast flatly and keeps the promise simple, that the exiles are not forgotten. Wesley takes little as size, a small sanctuary against the great temple, to which they may flee as a man flees to the horns of the altar, having in captivity the communion supposed possible only in the house.

Henry renders the phrase men of thy redemption and presses the irony that these kinsmen could redeem nothing, being captives themselves; he says the men of Jerusalem cut the exiles off from membership.

debates.question: Who are the brethren the prophet is told to think of?

positions.position: The exiles, his true kindred, to be regarded as such rather than the corrupt priests at Jerusalem.
His nearest kindred left behind in Jerusalem.

debates.question: What does a little sanctuary mean?

positions.position: Small in size, against the great temple.
Not an adjective at all: a sanctuary for a little while, for the term of the captivity.
Either a small sanctuary or a sanctuary of the few who were really his; the first is preferable for the contrast between visible splendour and hidden grace.

debates.question: What is the force of men of thy kindred?

positions.position: Men of thy redemption, the next of kin holding the right of redeeming an alienated possession.
An allusion to the office of the kinsman whose duty was to assist his ruined relative.

outliers.claim: Records that the Greek translators mistook the word and gave men of thy captivity, followed by the Syriac and Arabic, and reports Kimchi's view that the three phrases point to three separate deportations.

Turns the passage into a rule about recognising the Church: it is not to be measured by common opinion or by splendour, since men are drawn to ruin under the name of a church wherever the show is grand enough, while the true one is often preserved in hiding places among people of no estimation.

themes: Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,

Son of man, thy brethren, even thy brethren, the men of thy kindred, and all the house of Israel wholly, are they unto whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, Get you far from the Lord: unto us is this land given in possession.

Therefore say, Thus saith the Lord God; Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come.

17.pericope_label: Therefore say, Thus saith the Lord God; I will even gather you from the people, and assemble you out of the countries where ye have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel. And they shall come thither, and they shall take away all the detestable things thereof and all the abominations thereof from thence. And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh: That they may walk in my statutes, and keep mine ordinances, and do them: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will recompense their way upon their own heads, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the gift of the land against the exclusive claim of the men in the city, makes unity of purpose at once the consequence and the condition of the moral change, explains the stony heart as what is unnatural and incongruous in a man, and refuses to universalise the promise, since responsibility and the power of choice are not taken away and grace refused leaves a man worse rather than untouched.

Calvin treats the return as proof that the sanctuary promise was not empty and as the covenant resumed after an interruption, locates the reproach in a people who defiled a land dedicated to God, and warns that the zeal for purging must not be claimed as the people's own, since they could not leave their sins until renewed. Gill distinguishes the two senses of one heart, and says there is neither will nor power to walk in the statutes until the new heart is given.

Clarke reads the promise as a system of renewed affections with a new spirit to direct them, and makes the holiness of the life the proof of the work on the heart. Wesley alone keeps the whole promise on the ground, reading it of those who returned on the proclamations of two Persian kings and cleansed the temple of superstition.

debates.question: Is the promise of a new heart spiritual or historical?

positions.position: A moral and spiritual change, unity of purpose being consequence and condition together.
Regeneration, without which the people could not forsake their sins at all.
A whole system of renewed affections with a new spirit to direct them.
The historical return: a heart to go back under two Persian proclamations, and with one consent to rebuild and restore true religion.

debates.question: Who removes the abominations, and when?

positions.position: The returned exiles, chastened and purified; the shift from you to they may mean the work belonged to their children.
The Israelites after their return, whose sacrilege in defiling a land dedicated to God had caused the expulsion.
Those who came back on the two proclamations and abolished superstition from the temple.
Both an undivided heart, no longer halting between God and idols, and concord among them, an oneness of affection and judgment.
Unity of purpose, self-will being what divides and submission what unites.

outliers.claim: Guards the promise against merit: God had seemed to praise the people's zeal in purging the land, but the two things must be held together, that the elect attend strenuously to their duty and that they are nothing of themselves.
Records that the Greek and Arabic versions read another heart rather than one heart, a different one from what they had before.

themes: Therefore say, Thus saith the Lord God; I will even gather you from the people, and assemble you out of the countries where ye have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel.
And they shall come thither, and they shall take away all the detestable things thereof and all the abominations thereof from thence.
And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh:
That they may walk in my statutes, and keep mine ordinances, and do them: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will recompense their way upon their own heads, saith the Lord God.

22.pericope_label: Then did the cherubims lift up their wings, and the wheels beside them; and the glory of the God of Israel was over them above. And the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city, and stood upon the mountain which is on the east side of the city. Afterwards the spirit took me up, and brought me in a vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea, to them of the captivity. So the vision that I had seen went up from me. Then I spake unto them of the captivity all the things that the Lord had shewed me.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the mountain as the one later known for its olives, higher than the city and overlooking it entirely, and gathers what else belongs to it, a later prophet's vision of the Lord standing there in judgment, the incarnate Son's prediction of the second destruction, and the ascension; he says the report to the exiles was meant to show the vanity of trusting that the guilty city would be preserved.

Gill traces the glory out of the temple and then out of the city. Calvin meets the difficulty the departure creates, that God had promised to dwell there perpetually, by distinguishing an interruption from a broken promise; he holds the whole to have been vision and the prophet never to have left his place, argues it from the Spirit opening a faculty beyond natural sight, and explains why the report was needed by the exiles, who resented the prophets as much as the men at home despised the captives.

Clarke counts the stages of the departure as a proof of long-suffering, God leaving by little and little, and notes that the captives at first profited little by the report. Wesley says the mountain kept the glory within call, ready to return if even now they would understand the things that made for their peace.

Henry gives the reason for the pauses, that the glory found none to intercede and none to invite its return, and finds an irony in the place, since the same hill had carried their idols and was called the mount of corruption, so that God now sets his tribunal where they had set their affront.

debates.question: Why did the glory stop on that mountain?

positions.position: Because the idols set there had confronted God in his own house, so he now pitches his tribunal on the mount of corruption.
To remain within call and ready to return if even then they would understand the things belonging to their peace.
As one more stage in a departure made by little and little, before the final removal to heaven.
Because the hill overlooks the whole city; and the same place carries a later prophet's judgment vision, the prediction of the second destruction, and the ascension.

debates.question: Does the departure break the promise to dwell there perpetually?

positions.position: No: an interruption is not a breach, since the exile had a term and the worship was restored at its end, so the place remained sacred.

debates.question: Was the prophet bodily in Jerusalem?

positions.position: No: he never left his place, and being brought back by vision proves he had never bodily been there, though the point is not pressed on those who think otherwise.
The vision closed and the prophet was transported in spirit back into Chaldea to declare what he had seen.

outliers.claim: Raises against himself the objection that reporting the vision to the exiles was superfluous, since its lesson was for the people at home, and answers that the captives resented having to bear with prophets at all, so the warning was as necessary among them.
Reads the slowness of the departure as reluctance: God went gradually because he left unwillingly and would not have gone at all had they not forced him from them.
